headline: Halliday G2 smart glasses skip the camera for in-lens AI displays
summary: The new Halliday G2 smart glasses ditch cameras for AI-powered meeting assistance and real-time translation, featuring dual 600x300 micro-LED displays.
details: Halliday is launching its second-generation smart glasses, the G2, which forgo cameras in favor of advanced AI features and improved in-lens displays. The G2 aims to compete with devices like the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses by focusing on discreet intelligence and productivity.

Instead of the previous DigiWindow display, the Halliday G2 utilizes binocular waveguide displays with dual micro-LED projectors, offering 600x300 pixel resolution in each lens. These displays boast a brightness of 1,600 nits and are designed to be lightweight, with the glasses targeting a weight under 50 grams.

The headline AI feature, Meeting Flow, is designed to follow conversations, identify action points, and generate to-do lists, similar to the Even G2's Conversate feature. This builds on Halliday's previous Proactive AI, now specifically tailored for business activities.

The AI can display real-time captions, conduct quick research, provide context during breaks, and offer advice on decisions and unresolved items. The glasses also support real-time translation from 45 languages and access to the Halliday AI assistant.

Additional features include notifications, dashboard cards, reminders, and a 'Stealth mode' that dims the display for low-light environments. Unlike some competitors, Halliday has opted not to include a smart ring controller with the G2.

The Halliday G2 smart glasses will be available for pre-order starting July 21, with an expected price of $599. A $10 deposit secures a $100 discount, with prescription lenses available at an additional cost. Release is slated for September.

headline_marked: [[Z.ai powers 1GW AI data center]] using only Chinese chips, report claims
headline: Z.ai powers 1GW AI data center using only Chinese chips, report claims
summary: The GLM developer now operates multiple 10,000-chip clusters, marking a significant step in China's domestic AI hardware development.
details: Chinese AI firm Z.ai has reportedly completed and partially activated a 1-gigawatt (GW) data center, exclusively utilizing domestically produced chips. This facility is designed to train the company's GLM model family, with sources indicating Z.ai now manages several computing clusters each containing over 10,000 chips.

A 1GW capacity is substantial, equivalent to powering approximately 750,000 homes, positioning this data center among the largest developed by any Chinese AI laboratory. While the specific chip supplier remains unnamed, Z.ai's recent training history suggests Huawei's Ascend accelerators were used, as their GLM-5.2 model was reportedly trained without any Nvidia hardware.

Z.ai, formerly known as Zhipu, has been on the U.S. Commerce Department's entity list since January 2025, restricting its access to Nvidia silicon and making domestic alternatives its sole option. This development aligns with Beijing's plan to invest approximately 2 trillion yuan ($295 billion) over five years in a national network of AI data centers, with a goal of sourcing at least 80% of the underlying technology from Chinese suppliers.

However, challenges remain in chip production. China's most advanced stable node, SMIC's N+2 process, is operating at over 93% utilization. Furthermore, limited domestic High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) constrains the assembly of accelerators like Huawei's Ascend, with Huawei shipping around 812,000 AI chips last year. This means China can build the infrastructure for a 1GW data center faster than it can produce the chips required to power it.

Despite these production hurdles, Z.ai is experiencing significant financial growth, with projections of $1 billion in annual recurring revenue after achieving its 2026 sales target early. The company recently raised billions through a Hong Kong IPO and a subsequent share sale.
